decks.name: Tumors I: General, Syndromes, Gliomas & Nerve Sheath (Greenberg)

cards.text: Pediatric brain tumors are the most common **solid** tumor of childhood and second only to {{c1::leukemia}} among childhood cancers. The proportion that is **infratentorial** depends on age: 0–6 months {{c2::≈ 27%}}, 12–24 months {{c3::≈ 74%}}, 2–16 years {{c4::≈ 42%}}. In neonates the most common tumor is {{c5::teratoma}}.

cards.vorderseite: Brain tumors in the first year of life
cards.rueckseite:
≈ 8% of pediatric brain tumors; 90% neuroectodermal; most common neonatal tumor **teratoma**; also astrocytoma, choroid plexus tumors, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, AT/RT, desmoplastic infantile tumors.
Often very large at diagnosis (open sutures, plasticity).
**Presentation:** vomiting, **macrocrania**/bulging fontanelle, developmental arrest or regression, failure to thrive, seizures.

Oral **alkylating** prodrug (→ MTIC) that methylates guanine at **O6** and N7. **MGMT** repairs O6-methylguanine → tumors with **MGMT promoter methylation** (silenced MGMT) respond better.
**Side effects:** myelosuppression (especially **thrombocytopenia**), lymphopenia → **PCP prophylaxis** during concurrent chemoradiation, nausea, fatigue.
Can induce **hypermutation** in low-grade gliomas.
Other agents: nitrosoureas (BCNU, CCNU) cross the BBB well (pulmonary fibrosis, myelosuppression); BCNU wafers (Gliadel); PCV = procarbazine, CCNU, vincristine; bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) for recurrent GBM and radiation necrosis.

- **Lymphoma:** steroids before biopsy can make it nondiagnostic; lymphoma and small cell carcinoma need only biopsy, so a correct frozen diagnosis spares debulking
- **Low-grade glioma vs. reactive gliosis:** look for hypercellularity and secondary structures of Scherer (perineuronal/perivascular satellitosis, subpial spread)
- **Oligodendroglioma:** the "fried egg" halo is a formalin artifact, absent on frozen sections
- **Undergrading** from sampling; pilocytic astrocytoma can be overgraded
- **Radiation necrosis vs. recurrence:** often coexist
- **Tumefactive demyelination and infarct:** macrophages mimic glioma cells
- **Meningioma vs. schwannoma:** freezing artifact mimics Antoni B

cards.titel: Other genetic tumor syndromes with CNS tumors
zeilen: SHH medulloblastoma (TP53-mutant), choroid plexus carcinoma, high-grade glioma (children); IDH-mutant astrocytoma (20–40 y)
Hypermutated malignant gliomas, embryonal tumors; café-au-lait spots ("Turcot")

cards.rueckseite:
Multiple **non-vestibular schwannomas** (spinal, peripheral, cranial) with **pain** as the leading symptom; meningiomas less often.
**Genes:** **SMARCB1** or **LZTR1** (22q); NF2 is inactivated in the tumors, but not in the germline.
**Excluded if:** germline NF2 mutation, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or a first-degree relative with NF2.
(Unilateral vestibular schwannoma can occur with LZTR1.)

cards.text: The only well-established environmental risk factor for glioma is {{c1::ionizing radiation}}. In IDH-mutant astrocytoma, {{c2::homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion}} upgrades the tumor to **CNS WHO grade 4** even without necrosis or microvascular proliferation. All IDH-wildtype glioblastomas should be tested for {{c3::MGMT promoter methylation}}; 1p/19q must be tested in IDH-mutant gliomas unless {{c4::ATRX loss or TP53 mutation}} is present.

**5-ALA** (5-aminolevulinic acid) is metabolized to fluorescent {{c1::protoporphyrin IX}} in high-grade glioma cells. In the RCT, complete resection of enhancing tumor rose from {{c2::36% to 65%}} and 6-month PFS from 21% to {{c3::41%}}, without an effect on {{c4::overall survival}}.

cards.vorderseite: Gross total resection in diffuse glioma: definition and contraindications to aggressive surgery
cards.rueckseite:
**GTR definition:** enhancing tumor: removal of all enhancing (and enclosed non-enhancing) tumor on MRI **within 48 h**; non-enhancing tumor: removal of the T2/FLAIR abnormality.
Tumor cells extend beyond the visible margins, so GTR is not cure.
**Biopsy rather than resection favored:** elderly/poor medical condition, **KPS < 70**, multicentric tumors, deep or bilateral (butterfly) location, extensive eloquent involvement.
Awake mapping increases resection with fewer late deficits.

Early **maximal safe resection** is the first step (better survival and delayed malignant transformation than watchful waiting).
- **Low risk** (age < 40 and GTR): MRI surveillance every 3–6 months
- **High risk** (age > 40 or subtotal resection): **RT (50.4–54 Gy) followed by PCV** (**RTOG 9802**: PFS and OS benefit in IDH-mutant tumors) or RT + temozolomide
- Early RT prolongs PFS but **not OS** (EORTC 22845); dose escalation no benefit
- Newer option: **vorasidenib** (IDH1/2 inhibitor, INDIGO 2023) for residual/recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma after surgery alone
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 671–672 (vorasidenib added after the 10th edition)

cards.rueckseite:
**Pseudoprogression:** new or increased enhancement **≤ 3 months** after radiation + temozolomide, in up to 28–60%; more frequent with **MGMT-methylated** tumors; histologically like radiation necrosis. Rule: changes within 12 weeks and **inside the radiation field** are treated as pseudoprogression → repeat MRI. Symptomatic: steroids, **bevacizumab**, LITT.
**Pseudoresponse:** decreased enhancement from **anti-VEGF agents** (bevacizumab) or steroids that stabilize the BBB without true tumor shrinkage → follow T2/FLAIR.

zeilen: All enhancing disease gone for ≥ 4 weeks, no new lesions, stable/improved FLAIR, **off steroids**, clinically stable
≥ 50% decrease in the sum of products of perpendicular diameters for ≥ 4 weeks, no new lesions, steroids not increased
≥ 25% increase in enhancing lesions, significant FLAIR increase, any new lesion, or clinical deterioration
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 37.6, p. 675. Replaced the Macdonald criteria because enhancement alone is misleading.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Elderly / poor KPS:** hypofractionated RT (**40 Gy in 15 fractions**) + temozolomide improves survival over RT alone; **temozolomide alone** if MGMT methylated (Nordic, NOA-08); best supportive care if very frail
- **Tumor treating fields** (alternating electric fields, EF-14): added to maintenance temozolomide, median OS ≈ 21 vs. 16 months
- Recurrence: re-resection, lomustine, bevacizumab (PFS but not OS benefit), re-irradiation, trials
cards.notiz: Greenberg ch. 37 (treatment of grade 3–4 diffuse gliomas)

zeilen: Adolescents/young adults, cerebral hemispheres, poor prognosis
Children, long-standing **epilepsy**, cortical; **MYB::QKI** fusion; resection is curative
Young patients with epilepsy, calcified temporal lesion, BRAF V600E / FGFR
Adults, **anterior third ventricle/lamina terminalis**, **PRKCA** mutation; hypothalamic morbidity with resection
Posterior fossa adults, methylation-defined, MAPK + CDKN2A/B loss, aggressive
Periventricular cerebral hemisphere, cyst with nodule, PRKCA fusion
Children, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, small cysts, hydrocephalus; KIAA1549::BRAF + 1p deletion
Adults, cluster of small T2-bright nodules in deep cortex/subcortical white matter ("bubbly"); **leave alone** unless epileptogenic
Like central neurocytoma but in the parenchyma
Adults, cerebellum, lipidized neuronal cells; recurs

cards.rueckseite:
**Filum terminale / conus** of adults (most common tumor of the filum); now **CNS WHO grade 2** (WHO 2021).
Histology: papillae with **myxoid** perivascular stroma, GFAP+.
Clinic: back pain, sciatica, sphincter dysfunction; can present with SAH or superficial siderosis.
**Treatment:** **en bloc resection** without violating the capsule (piecemeal removal → CSF seeding and recurrence); RT for residual or disseminated disease. Image the whole neuraxis.

Loss of speech after cerebellar injury, typically **1–2 days after resection of a posterior fossa tumor in a child** (11–29% overall; medulloblastoma 53%, ependymoma 33%, pilocytic 11%); ≈ 1% in adults.
Often with ataxia, hypotonia, **irritability/emotional lability**; posterior fossa syndrome adds cranial nerve deficits and urinary dysfunction.
Risk factors: midline/vermian tumor, brainstem involvement, vermian split; thought to involve the **dentato-thalamo-cortical** pathway (superior cerebellar peduncles).
Speech returns (usually as dysarthria) over weeks to months, rarely to normal.

zeilen: Into the CPA, not reaching the brainstem
Reaches the brainstem surface without displacing it
Displaces the brainstem and cranial nerves
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 45.7, p. 784. Koos IV usually needs surgery; small tumors: observation or radiosurgery.

cards.vorderseite: Vestibular schwannoma: serviceable hearing and screening
cards.rueckseite:
**Serviceable hearing:** Gardner–Robertson class I–II or AAO-HNS class A–B (**"50/50 rule"**: pure-tone average ≤ 50 dB and speech discrimination ≥ 50%; some use 30 dB/70%).
**MRI indicated for:** interaural difference ≥ 10 dB at ≥ 2 frequencies or ≥ 15 dB at one, asymmetric tinnitus, sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
Small tumors also get ENG/VEMP (superior/inferior vestibular nerve) and ABR (predicts hearing preservation).

- **Retrosigmoid (suboccipital):** any size, **hearing preservation possible**; lateral IAC fundus hard to see; postoperative headache
- **Translabyrinthine:** any size, **sacrifices hearing**, early facial nerve identification at the fundus, little cerebellar retraction
- **Middle fossa:** small **intracanalicular** tumors with good hearing (≤ 1–1.5 cm in the CPA); temporal lobe retraction, facial nerve lies superior and at risk

Facial nerve outcome depends mainly on **tumor size**; it is usually displaced **anteriorly** (and superiorly).

Benign tumor of **perineurial cells** (EMA+, S100−, claudin-1+).
- **Intraneural:** adolescents/young adults, progressive painless **mononeuropathy** (often sciatic/peroneal, radial), fusiform enlargement with "onion bulb" whorls on biopsy; fascicular biopsy for diagnosis, usually no resection (would sacrifice the nerve)
- **Soft-tissue (extraneural):** subcutaneous mass
